Oh no, months of that sounds exhausting. I'm sorry it's been so rough. If you really want to quit, I'm on your side. But could you give it a few days before you hand anything in? Decisions made at the end of a bad week tend to look different on Monday. Is it the work itself, your manager, or something else? And do you have enough savings to get by for a while if you leave before finding something new? Want to call tonight and talk it through?

## 2

I can tell you've thought about this, so I'll give you reasons you can check yourself instead of asking you to trust NASA. When a ship sails away, the hull disappears before the mast, which is what happens when something drops over a curve. During a lunar eclipse, the Earth's shadow on the Moon is always round, from every angle. People in Australia see different stars than people in Canada, and it's daytime in one country while it's night in another. Around 240 BC, a Greek scholar named Eratosthenes worked out the Earth's size from the shadows of two sticks in different cities, and you can repeat his experiment with a friend in another town. Which of those seems weakest to you? I'm happy to dig into it.

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it's actually all the colours of the rainbow mixed together. Each colour is a wave of light, and blue light has shorter waves than red light.

On its way to your eyes, sunlight passes through air, which is full of tiny nitrogen and oxygen molecules. When light hits these molecules, some of it bounces off in random directions. This is called scattering. Short waves scatter much more than long ones: blue light scatters about five to six times more than red. So blue light gets bounced all over the sky, and wherever you look, some of it is heading toward you. That's why the whole sky glows blue.

You might ask why the sky isn't violet, since violet waves are even shorter. The sun gives off less violet than blue, and our eyes are less sensitive to violet, so blue wins.

At sunset, the light travels through much more air to reach you. Most of the blue gets scattered away before it arrives, leaving the oranges and reds.

夜里十一点，雨还没有停。雨点打在窗外的铁皮雨棚上，一阵密，一阵疏，像有人在远处不紧不慢地敲鼓。楼下的路灯被雨丝裹着，光晕散开，昏黄得有些模糊。偶尔一辆车驶过，轮胎碾过积水，哗的一声，又很快被雨声盖住。我关了灯，坐在窗边，空气里有泥土和青苔的潮味。手边的茶早就凉了，书也停在同一页。这样的夜晚好像什么都不用做，只要听着雨，让一天的疲惫慢慢沉下去。
